title: Exploration
text:
This exploration examines delivery_days (days from order purchase to customer delivery) as a single numeric target using the cleaned dataset (data/df_master_clean.rds) from data.qmd. We start with the target distribution, then move through grouped summaries, monthly trends, and predictor relationships, ending with one number-backed decision, data limitations, and the transition to Milestone 2 modeling.
Any column derived from delivery outcomes or post-delivery status—such as delayed_days or delivered_status—reflects the outcome after the fact and is excluded as a predictor for delivery_days.


Code
library(tidyverse)
library(lubridate)
library(knitr)

df_master <- read_rds("data/df_master_clean.rds")

title: Exploration
text:
## Part 1: Basic EDA — Target (delivery_days) Distribution
Before looking at predictors or subgroups, we inspect delivery_days directly to see its center, spread, and skew across all cleaned order items.


Code
target_stats <- df_master |>
  summarise(
    min_days = min(delivery_days),
    mean_days = mean(delivery_days),
    median_days = median(delivery_days),
    max_days = max(delivery_days),
    sd_days = sd(delivery_days),
    n_rows = n(),
    n_orders = n_distinct(order_id)
  )

kable(
  target_stats,
  digits = 2,
  format.args = list(big.mark = ","),
  col.names = c("Min", "Mean", "Median", "Max", "SD", "Rows", "Unique Orders"),
  caption = "Summary statistics for delivery_days in class order"
)

  geom_histogram(bins = 50, fill = "#2b8cbe", color = "white", alpha = 0.9) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = median(df_master$delivery_days), linetype = "dashed", color = "#d95f02", linewidth = 0.9) +

Distribution of delivery_days across cleaned order items, with vertical markers for median and mean.




Because 12 mean days exceeds 10 median days and reaches up to 209 days, evaluating median and tail behavior alongside mean error will matter when modeling delivery_days

2.2 Purchase Month Trend
Because orders span multiple months, we check whether monthly delivery times shift over the purchase timeline Monthly mean delivery_days will vary across months and rise during higher-volume / seasonal periods rather than staying flat.


Code
monthly_tbl <- df_master |>
  group_by(purchase_year_month) |>
  summarise(
    mean_days = mean(delivery_days),
    median_days = median(delivery_days),
    n_orders = n_distinct(order_id),
    .groups = "drop"
  ) |>
  arrange(purchase_year_month)

slowest_mo <- monthly_tbl |> slice_max(mean_days, n = 1)
fastest_mo <- monthly_tbl |> slice_min(mean_days, n = 1)

ggplot(monthly_tbl, aes(x = purchase_year_month, y = mean_days)) +
  geom_line(color = "#2b8cbe", linewidth = 1) +
  geom_point(color = "#08519c", size = 2) +
  labs(
    title = "Monthly Mean Delivery Days Shift Across Time and Peak in Late 2017 / Early 2018",
    subtitle = "Mean delivery_days by purchase month",
    x = "Purchase Month",
    y = "Mean Delivery Days"
  ) +
  theme_minimal()









Monthly mean delivery_days ranges from 4 days (2016-12) to 54 days (2016-09), confirming that purchase_month / timing is a meaningful feature to include in Milestone 2.


2.3 Customer State vs. Delivery Days
Alongside seller state, we inspect how delivery duration varies by customer destination state (customer_state). Orders delivered to southeastern states such as SP will average fewer delivery days than orders shipped to distant northern/northeastern states.


Code
cust_state_tbl <- df_master |>
  group_by(customer_state) |>
  summarise(
    mean_days = mean(delivery_days),
    median_days = median(delivery_days),
    n_orders = n_distinct(order_id),
    .groups = "drop"
  ) |>
  arrange(desc(mean_days))

top_cust_slow <- cust_state_tbl |> slice_max(mean_days, n = 1)
sp_cust <- cust_state_tbl |> filter(customer_state == "SP")

ggplot(cust_state_tbl, aes(x = reorder(customer_state, mean_days), y = mean_days)) +
  geom_col(fill = "#41b6c4") +
  coord_flip() +
  labs(
    title = "Customer States Far From Southeastern Hubs Average Substantially Longer Delivery",
    subtitle = "Mean delivery_days across customer_state",
    x = "Customer State",
    y = "Mean Delivery Days"
  ) +
  theme_minimal()









Customer deliveries in SP average 8.3 days across 40,495 orders, compared with 27.8 days in RR (41 orders).


2.4 Product Weight & Freight Value vs. Delivery Days
Finally, we check how item weight (product_weight_g) and freight cost (freight_value) relate to delivery_days. Heavier items and higher-freight shipments will correspond to longer average delivery times and higher shipping charges


Code
weight_freight_tbl <- df_master |>
  mutate(
    weight_group = case_when(
      product_weight_g < 500 ~ "Light (<500g)",
      product_weight_g < 2000 ~ "Medium (500g–2kg)",
      product_weight_g < 10000 ~ "Heavy (2kg–10kg)",
      TRUE ~ "Very Heavy (10kg+)"
    ),
    weight_group = factor(weight_group, levels = c("Light (<500g)", "Medium (500g–2kg)", "Heavy (2kg–10kg)", "Very Heavy (10kg+)"))
  ) |>
  group_by(weight_group) |>
  summarise(
    mean_freight_brl = mean(freight_value),
    mean_days = mean(delivery_days),
    median_days = median(delivery_days),
    n_rows = n(),
    .groups = "drop"
  )

kable(
  weight_freight_tbl,
  digits = 2,
  format.args = list(big.mark = ","),
  col.names = c("Weight Group", "Mean Freight (BRL)", "Mean Days", "Median Days", "Rows"),

title: Exploration
text:
Decision, Limitations, and Next Steps (Milestone 2)
Adopt route- and weight-aware delivery buffers rather than a single flat delivery promise—for example, accounting for multi-week differences between SP (8.3 mean customer days) and distant states such as RR (27.8 mean days), as well as heavier 10kg+ shipments (14.9 mean days)
### Limitations * Historical scope & missing timestamps: The Olist dataset covers 2016–2018 operations and omits orders lacking recorded delivery dates, so estimates may not reflect current carrier routing or unfulfilled orders. * Small counts in remote states & non-predictive outcome fields: Low order counts in remote states increase variance of raw averages, and post-delivery fields (delayed_days, delivered_status) are excluded from feature exploration to avoid leakage.

title: Home
text: How do delivery time, shipping cost, and product characteristics shape the customer experience at Olist, and when do orders miss the delivery promise?

title: Home
text: How do delivery time, shipping cost, and product characteristics shape the customer experience at Olist, and when do orders miss the delivery promise?

title: Home
text:
Why this matters
Olist is a Brazilian online marketplace that connects small sellers to customers across the country. Delivery speed and shipping cost are central to customer satisfaction, and they are set by logistics: where the seller and customer are, how heavy the item is, and what category it belongs to. About two years of order data (2016-2018) can show where the delivery promise holds, where it breaks, and what drives shipping costs.
Use the navbar: Data and Exploration are the analysis, covering the order-level dataset (about 110K item rows), the calculated fields I built (delivery status, total cost, time-of-day features), and the plots that compare delivery time, freight, weight, and category. The remaining pages cover the file format, the presentation slides, and the GitHub and Netlify setup.

title: Home
text:
What I found so far

About 90% of orders arrive earlier than estimated, so Olist’s delivery estimates are conservative.
Purchase timing (weekday vs. weekend, time of day) barely changes delivery outcomes.
Location and product type matter more: delivery time varies by customer state and by category, and heavier items cost more to ship.

Step 1: Loading the Six Raw Olist Tables
Read the six raw CSV files (customers, category_translation, order_items, orders, products, and sellers)


Code
customers <- read_csv("data/customers.csv", show_col_types = FALSE)
category_translation <- read_csv("data/category_translation.csv", show_col_types = FALSE)
order_items <- read_csv("data/order_items.csv", show_col_types = FALSE)
orders <- read_csv("data/orders.csv", show_col_types = FALSE)
products <- read_csv("data/products.csv", show_col_types = FALSE)
sellers <- read_csv("data/sellers.csv", show_col_types = FALSE)

raw_table_summary <- tibble(
  table_name = c("order_items", "orders", "customers", "products", "sellers", "category_translation"),
  rows = c(nrow(order_items), nrow(orders), nrow(customers), nrow(products), nrow(sellers), nrow(category_translation)),
  columns = c(ncol(order_items), ncol(orders), ncol(customers), ncol(products), ncol(sellers), ncol(category_translation)),
  primary_key = c("order_id + order_item_id", "order_id", "customer_id", "product_id", "seller_id", "product_category_name")
)

title: Data
section: Step 2: Joining the Six Tables into One Master Dataset
text:
Step 2: Joining the Six Tables into One Master Dataset
Starts from order_items and joins orders, customers, products, category_translation, and sellers via left_join(), comparing row counts before and after joining to verify there is no row multiplication.


Code
rows_before_join <- nrow(order_items)

df_master <- order_items |>
  left_join(orders, by = "order_id") |>
  left_join(customers, by = "customer_id") |>
  left_join(products, by = "product_id") |>
  left_join(category_translation, by = "product_category_name") |>
  left_join(sellers, by = "seller_id")

rows_after_join <- nrow(df_master)

join_check <- tibble(
  stage = c("Before joins (order_items)", "After joining all 6 tables (df_master)"),
  rows = c(rows_before_join, rows_after_join),
  columns = c(ncol(order_items), ncol(df_master))
)

kable(
  join_check,
  format.args = list(big.mark = ","),
  col.names = c("Pipeline Stage", "Row Count", "Column Count"),
  caption = "Row-count validation before and after merging the six Olist tables"
)

Joining the six tables keeps 112,650 rows (matching 112,650 rows in order_items) across 33 columns, confirming zero row inflation during the merges.

Step 3: Auditing Missing Values and Cleaning Rules
Audits missing values across all columns of df_master, fixes column spelling typos, creates purchase_year_month, filters out rows missing delivery_days, and imputes missing product categories and numeric product dimensions.


Code

  column = names(df_master),
  missing_count = colSums(is.na(df_master)),
  missing_pct = round(100 * colSums(is.na(df_master)) / nrow(df_master), 2)
) |>
  filter(missing_count > 0) |>
  arrange(desc(missing_count))

  na_before,
  format.args = list(big.mark = ","),

Code
rows_initial <- nrow(df_master)
missing_del_n <- sum(is.na(df_master$delivery_days))

df_master <- df_master |>
  rename(
    product_name_length = product_name_lenght,
    product_description_length = product_description_lenght
  ) |>
  mutate(
    purchase_year_month = make_date(purchase_year, purchase_month, 1)
  ) |>
  filter(!is.na(delivery_days))

rows_after_target_filter <- nrow(df_master)

df_master <- df_master |>
  mutate(
    product_category_name = if_else(is.na(product_category_name), "unknown", product_category_name),
    product_category_name_english = if_else(
      is.na(product_category_name_english),
      product_category_name,
      product_category_name_english
    ),
    across(
      c(
        product_name_length,
        product_description_length,
        product_photos_qty,
        product_weight_g,
        product_length_cm,
        product_height_cm,
        product_width_cm
      ),
      ~ if_else(is.na(.x), median(.x, na.rm = TRUE), .x)
    )
  )




Summary of Cleaning Decisions (One Sentence per Rule)

Column name & date standardization: Corrected the raw typos (product_name_lenght -> product_name_length and product_description_lenght -> product_description_length) and built purchase_year_month so naming is consistent and monthly trends can be tracked cleanly.
Missing target removal: Removed 2,454 rows (2.18%) missing delivery_days—moving from 112,650 to 110,196 rows—because records without an observed delivery duration cannot train or evaluate a delivery_days model.
Category missingness ("unknown"): Filled missing product_category_name and product_category_name_english entries with "unknown" rather than dropping rows so uncategorized items still contribute shipping, timing, and geographic records.
Numeric product spec imputation (median): Imputed missing values across the seven numeric product specification columns (product_name_length, product_description_length, product_photos_qty, product_weight_g, product_length_cm, product_height_cm, and product_width_cm) using each column’s median because product dimensions and counts are skewed and the median resists extreme outliers.

After cleaning, 0 missing values remain across all 34 columns in 110,196 rows (96,476 unique orders).


Step 4: Baseline Sanity Checks (Status, Target Summary, Timing, and Geography)
Checks order statuses and cancellation rate, overall delivery_days statistics, purchase day/month coverage, and seller-state delivery patterns before moving to exploration.

title: Data
section: Step 5: Saving the Cleaned Dataset and Next Step
text:
Step 5: Saving the Cleaned Dataset and Next Step
Saves the cleaned df_master dataset to data/df_master_clean.rds so downstream pages load a consistent, validated dataset.
With df_master_clean.rds saved, the Exploration page examines delivery_days directly first, then tests relationships across geography, purchase month, shipping cost, and product characteristics before closing with a data backed decision and limitations.
